blocks.html: Every time you get on the internet, you are not alone. Before you protect yourself, it helps to know who is actually watching:

items.title: Wi-Fi Operator
items.html: Whoever runs the network you're connected to — a coffee shop, an office, a landlord.

items.title: Your ISP
items.html: Your Internet Service Provider (Optimum, Verizon, and the like) sees every unencrypted request you make.

items.title: Lawful Interception
items.html: Government or law enforcement requests, made through legal channels.

items.title: Unlawful Interception
items.html: Hackers and other bad actors who want your data for their own purposes.

blocks.html: The uncomfortable truth: you are always being watched. An unencrypted connection can leak your IP address, and your IP address can reveal your physical location — so network privacy is about physical safety too, not just data. A quick tell: look at the start of a web address. HTTP versus HTTPS, where the S stands for secure. You want the S.

A VPN connects you to another computer somewhere else in the world through an encrypted tunnel, and you borrow that computer's IP address instead of the one your ISP handed you. It doesn't make your activity disappear — it makes it much harder to link back to you. Does privacy even matter anymore? Yes, and the earlier you start, the better: on the internet, companies and corporations are waiting to consume you.

You → Website (normally) →
Website sees your real IP address →
You → VPN Server → Website (with a VPN) →
Website sees the VPN's IP, not yours.

subsections.title: Terminology
subsections.summary: The words you will run into.

items.title: IP address
items.html: The number that identifies your connection online. It can reveal your rough location.

items.title: ISP
items.html: Your internet service provider. It can see every site you connect to unless you hide it.

items.title: DNS
items.html: The internet’s phone book, turning names into IP addresses. Encrypted DNS (DoH) keeps lookups private.

items.title: HTTPS
items.html: Encrypted web traffic — the padlock. Others can see which site you visit, but not what you do there.

items.title: Tor
items.html: A network that bounces your traffic through three volunteer relays so sites can’t see who you are.

items.title: Router
items.html: The box that connects your home to the internet. Change its default password and keep it updated.

items.title: VPN
items.html: A virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel from your device to a server, which then reaches the web for you.

items.title: VPS
items.html: A virtual private server: a rented slice of a server you fully control, for self-hosting.

items.title: No-logs policy
items.html: A provider’s promise not to record what you do. Look for independent audits.

items.title: Kill switch
items.html: Blocks all traffic if the VPN drops, so nothing leaks outside the tunnel.

items.title: DNS / IPv6 leak
items.html: When some requests skip the tunnel and reveal your real provider or address.

lede: Who's actually watching your traffic, how a VPN protects you (and where it can't), how to pick a provider you can trust, and how to run your own VPN or website on a rented server.
